title: Coding Agent Benchmarks Miss the Hard Part
description: Passing coding tasks is not the same as safely shipping changes. A practical look at what agent benchmarks reveal, what they leave out, and how to test a coding agent yourself.
coverAlt: A small code patch floating above a sprawling software system
lede: An agent can close a benchmark issue and still be the teammate you do not trust with your repository. The missing part lives between passing tests and owning the change.

sections.title: Issue resolution is a useful slice
paragraphs: SWE-bench asks a model to resolve real GitHub issues in a repository, then checks whether the patch passes tests. That is a concrete, valuable task. Verified narrows the benchmark with human filtering because some original tasks were ambiguous or did not reliably test the requested fix.

But passing the provided tests is not a complete definition of responsible software work. Tests may miss a regression. The patch may implement a brittle workaround. A human maintainer might reject an answer that technically passes but ignores project conventions or expands the change unnecessarily.
The benchmark measures a slice of work under a specific environment. It says something useful about that slice. The mistake is promoting it into 'this agent can do software engineering'.

sections.title: The agent is bigger than the model
paragraphs: The system includes the model, prompt, tools, context management, retry policy, sandbox, and budget. Give a model search and terminal tools and it can inspect a repository in ways a bare prompt cannot. Change the harness and the outcome may change even when model weights stay fixed.

That makes benchmark comparison harder. Reports should name the full configuration and resource limits. How much wall time? How many model calls? Could it run tests repeatedly? Did it receive a prepared description or discover files itself? Without these details the reader cannot tell whether the advantage came from reasoning, scaffolding, or simply more attempts.

rows: The patch met the supplied tests
Solves examples under the stated setup
Lower time for successful benchmark runs
Cost, retries, setup or review time
Whether it used relevant context well

sections.title: Software quality has more than one axis
paragraphs: A useful local evaluation asks whether a patch is correct, small enough, readable, secure, and easy to maintain. It also asks what it costs to get there. Count the first-pass success rate and the number of interventions. Record when a model edits unrelated files, invents APIs, or claims to run checks it did not run.

Review the failed cases carefully. An agent that fails loudly is safer than one that confidently hides failure. A green score can cover a dangerous false success, such as a test weakened to pass. Your evaluator needs to notice those behaviours, not just whether a task ended with a patch.
bullets: Use recent issues from your codebase, after removing private material.
Freeze the repository state, tools, prompt, model version, and time limit.
Score test results, patch quality, unrequested edits, and human review time.
Keep original and hidden tests so the agent cannot pass by memorizing a task.
Track cost and failure severity alongside completion.

sections.title: Where the number belongs
paragraphs: Benchmark scores help shortlist tools and generate questions. They do not answer whether an agent fits your codebase. Use the benchmark to locate capability, then run the same controlled task set on your work and review its patches like you would review any new contributor.

If the agent saves a developer fifteen minutes but creates twenty minutes of cleanup, its benchmark reputation does not rescue the economics. If it produces a safe first draft that an engineer can validate quickly, even a lower benchmark score may be irrelevant to its usefulness.
The hard part is not a model writing code. It is knowing whether the change should be there, and taking responsibility when the answer is wrong.

title: RAG vs Long Context: Choose by Failure Mode
description: A clear engineering guide to retrieval-augmented generation and long context windows, with a decision framework based on freshness, corpus size, citations, and failure cost.
coverAlt: A branching path between a library index and a long open scroll
lede: The question is not whether RAG is dead. The question is what your system should do when the answer is missing, stale, or buried in a document it never retrieved.

sources.title: Lost in the Middle: How Language Models Use Long Contexts

sections.title: These are two ways to supply context
paragraphs: Long context means putting a large chunk of source material directly into a model request. Retrieval augmented generation searches a collection first, then places selected passages beside the question. Both try to give a model evidence it did not learn during training. Neither guarantees that the model will use that evidence correctly.

A bigger context window reduces the need to build an indexing pipeline for some tasks. A small changing set of documents can be simpler to pass directly. RAG can lower repeated token costs, search a much larger corpus, and return specific source locations. The trade is that retrieval introduces its own chance to miss the one passage the answer depends on.

sections.title: Pick based on your main failure mode
paragraphs: If a user needs a complete comparison across four short contracts, passing all four may be more reliable than hoping a retriever finds every relevant clause. If there are millions of support articles that change every day, searching and then supplying a few sources is usually more practical than sending the entire library on every request.

A paper from Liu and colleagues found that model performance can drop when relevant information appears in the middle of long inputs. The finding cautions against assuming a large context window is uniformly usable. It does not prove that every current model fails in exactly the same way. Test with your model and your documents.

rows: A few stable documents in full
Missed or contradictory detail across files
Recall of the exact supporting passage
Whether all necessary context survives packing

sections.title: Hybrid systems are normal, not a failure
paragraphs: You can retrieve candidate documents, rerank them, and then include full text from the few documents that need deep comparison. You can use long context for an individual session and retrieval across many sessions. The architecture should respond to evidence about failures, rather than ideology about which approach has won.

Do not start by creating embeddings because a tutorial did. Take twenty real questions and mark which source passages an expert would need. See whether direct context works. Build retrieval only when the corpus or measured quality requires it. Keep the retrieval results visible so a reviewer can tell whether the model had its evidence.

sections.title: An evaluation small enough to start today
paragraphs: Write twelve questions from the tasks people actually ask. Include three questions whose answer is absent, three where a newer policy contradicts an older one, and three requiring information from two sources. Record the acceptable answer and exact source passages before testing.

For each architecture, record whether the correct passage reached the model, whether the answer was supported by that passage, whether citations resolved to the right place, and how long the request took. If both approaches work, choose the simpler one. If retrieval misses, improve chunking or search before asking the model to hallucinate around absent evidence.
The right architecture is the one whose important failures you can see, reproduce, and fix.

title: Write Technical Posts Without AI Slop
description: A practical workflow for writing original technical content that uses AI without losing your examples, judgement, evidence, or natural voice.
coverAlt: A hand-written field note on a clean desk beside a silent typewriter
lede: Good technical writing starts with the detail you almost removed because it seemed too specific. That detail is usually the part nobody else can make up for you.

sources.title: Google Search Central: generative AI content

sections.title: Collect the material before you write the hook
paragraphs: Start with a small record: what you tried, what happened, what you expected, and what surprised you. If you are explaining a paper, write down the experimental setup and one limitation. If you are describing a build, capture the command, screenshot, or test result that grounds the account.

Do not ask a model for the post before you have this material. It will happily produce an elegant narrative that accidentally turns guesses into events. Your notes create a boundary between what you know, what you infer, and what you are still asking.

sections.title: Give AI an editing job, not your identity
paragraphs: A useful instruction is small: 'Find the sentence where I stop explaining why this benchmark result matters.' Or 'List the factual claims here that need a primary source.' That gives the model something it can do without pretending to be the author of your experience.

Ask for objections and uncertainty, then choose which ones matter. Do not accept false balance automatically. If the evidence supports a sharp conclusion, keep it. If it is ambiguous, say exactly where. Avoid letting the model flatten the voice into smooth generic phrasing just because the grammar looks clean.
sections.code:
1. Write raw notes from a real event, artifact, result, or question.
2. Mark each claim: observed / sourced / inferred / unknown.
3. Use AI to inspect structure, gaps, or objections.
4. Check citations and personal details yourself.
5. Read aloud and remove any sentence you would never say.

sections.title: Choose one thing worth saying
paragraphs: A post cannot carry every thought about a release. Choose the specific consequence for the reader. For a new speech model, maybe the useful question is whether it can transcribe a long English recording locally on available hardware. For an AI benchmark, maybe the issue is how a leaderboard changed the tool configuration between model versions.

Your opening can be surprising, but it should promise a payoff that the body actually delivers. Draft three versions, keep the strongest defensible one, then make sure the first paragraph identifies the subject quickly. A catchy opening that hides the topic is friction, not craft.

sections.title: Edit for the human details
paragraphs: Cut unsupported claims, stock transitions, and filler that could be pasted into a post about any product. Keep a small concrete moment if it clarifies the mechanism. It could be an exact error message or the awkward step a benchmark setup left out. Never invent a meeting, customer, failure, quote, or personal result to make the story warmer.

End where the implication lands. A simple consequence or practical next step often carries more force than a motivational moral or a question added to harvest comments. The reader does not need to agree to receive value from the post.
You can use AI and still write something worth reading. The test is whether there is a human choice in the result about what is important and why.

title: The Real Cost of AI Work
description: Measure AI project cost in retries, review, latency, maintenance and errors. A practical worksheet to decide whether a feature is earning its complexity.
coverAlt: A compact AI circuit balanced over handwritten cost notes
lede: That cheap model call is not the cheapest part of your AI feature. The expensive part is explaining the answer it got confidently wrong.

sources.title: Google SRE Book: Monitoring Distributed Systems

sections.title: The bill is the visible part
paragraphs: A model API gives you an invoice, and invoices are easy to count. But a product feature costs the time spent writing prompts, building retrieval, measuring bad answers, handling retries, and maintaining the integration when the provider changes its behaviour.

There is also the review queue. If a person needs to check every generated summary for unsupported claims, the product's cost includes that person's time. The feature may still be worthwhile, but compare the full task before and after AI instead of treating tokens as the whole budget.

sections.title: Make a rough cost model
paragraphs: Estimate total expense over a representative batch, such as one hundred user requests. Include model usage, search or tools, retries, human review, and repair. Track a range, not a false-precision number: the slow tail of requests and the hardest failures can dominate the user's experience.

sections.title: Measure before you scale
paragraphs: Collect normal tasks and failure-prone cases. Run a baseline workflow and the AI-assisted workflow with the same input. Record completion, correctness, latency, and review time. A language model that is slightly worse but much faster may fit a low-risk brainstorming task. It might be unacceptable in an action that sends money or changes an account.

Track uncertainty. One hundred requests from a few friendly testers can miss the uncommon but consequential case. If the system acts externally, count and review every action while you are still learning its behaviour. Gate actions behind confirmation until you know what mistakes it makes.

sections.title: Know when to keep the feature
paragraphs: An AI feature earns its place if it measurably improves a task someone wants to complete, with failure costs and maintenance that are acceptable. The improvement could be less waiting, access for a user who could not do the task before, or a better first draft. It does not have to make every metric better.

If a fixed rule, search box, or template handles the task more consistently, use the boring tool. You can keep the model for cases where flexible language matters. Product judgement includes knowing when a feature's demonstration is more impressive than its day-to-day value.
When you do ship it, keep a change log, a representative regression set, an owner, and a way to fall back. That is how an interesting prototype becomes a tool somebody can rely on.
